entities.name: Benedikt Kuripečič
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Benedikt Kuripečič (also spelled Kuripešić), a Slovene diplomat and travel writer of the early 16th century, is primarily remembered for his detailed ethnographic observations of the Ottoman Balkans and his pivotal role in transmitting the epic traditions surrounding the Battle of Kosovo to a wider European audience. Serving as an interpreter and secretary during a diplomatic mission from Ferdinand I, Archduke of Austria, to the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1530, Kuripečič's journey through Serbia and Bosnia provided him a unique vantage point on the cultural landscape of the region under Ottoman rule, making his account a rare and invaluable primary source for early modern Balkan history and folklore.

His magnum opus, 'Itinerarium Wegra. Auf den Weg. Kayserlicher Maiestat Legation von Ofen gen Constantinopel' (1531), meticulously documents the diplomatic party's route from Buda to Constantinople. Beyond mere itinerary, Kuripečič's narrative vividly describes the peoples, customs, and geopolitical realities of the Ottoman frontier provinces. Crucially, he recorded the oral traditions and epic songs concerning Miloš Obilić, the legendary Serbian knight who, according to folklore, assassinated Sultan Murad I at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Kuripečič's account is one of the earliest written records of these narratives, predating many South Slavic textualizations, and offers insights into the enduring cultural memory of the medieval Serbian Empire among its descendants.

entities.summary:
Benedikt Kuripečič (c. 1490, Gornji Grad – unknown), a Slovene diplomat and writer of the early 16th century, holds a singular place in the annals of South Slavic cultural history as one of the earliest recorded transmitters of epic poetry concerning the Battle of Kosovo and its heroes, particularly Miloš Obilić. His detailed travelogue, *Itinerarium Wegrayss Key. May. potschafft gen Constantinopel* (1531), offers an invaluable firsthand account of the Balkan lands under Ottoman rule, serving as a vital ethnographic and geopolitical document from a period of intense imperial flux. Kuripečič's journey in 1530-1531 as a translator and secretary within Ferdinand I's Habsburg embassy to Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent not only provided a diplomatic conduit but also a unique lens through which to observe the cultural landscape of the Ottoman Balkans.

During his arduous overland journey from Ljubljana to Constantinople, Kuripečič meticulously documented the diverse peoples, customs, and geographical features encountered. His keen observations extended to the oral traditions prevalent among the Serbs, Croats, and Bosnians he met, noting their preservation of heroic songs. Crucially, he recorded their veneration for Miloš Obilić, the legendary knight who assassinated Sultan Murad I at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, and described the epic narratives surrounding this pivotal event. This act of transcription, embedded within a diplomatic report, inadvertently preserved fragments of a rich oral tradition that would later become foundational to South Slavic national identities and literary movements.
